codes.label: Payback period and net return
codes.definition: Compare the realistic increase in earnings after the degree against the full cost, including tuition, fees, interest, taxes and lost income, to see how many years it takes to recoup the investment and whether it is worth it.

codes.label: Net cost after employer support
codes.definition: Look at what the program costs after employer reimbursement or tuition aid, relative to current salary, rather than the sticker price.

codes.label: Reimbursement terms and strings
codes.definition: Confirm in writing whether employer reimbursement is guaranteed for the full program, taxable, conditional on grades or tenure, subject to clawback if you leave, or could be cut.

codes.label: Foregone and lost income
codes.definition: Count income given up during the program, such as shift differentials, overtime, unpaid clinical or leave time, reduced hours, delayed raises and missed retirement compounding, as part of the true cost.

codes.label: Financing and debt burden
codes.definition: Consider how the money would be raised, whether savings or loans, and what interest rates, repayment terms and monthly payments would do to the budget and future borrowing.

codes.label: Competing financial commitments
codes.definition: Weigh how the program's cost competes for the same savings and cash flow as other near-term obligations such as a wedding, emergency fund, home purchase, children's college costs or retirement contributions.

codes.label: Emergency fund and financial cushion
codes.definition: Assess whether savings and reserves can absorb a job loss, illness, income gap or program setback without destabilizing the household.

codes.label: Single-earner household risk
codes.definition: A sole earner with dependents has no second income or co-parent to absorb shocks, so a fallback plan and support for emergencies are needed.

codes.label: Alternative and external funding
codes.definition: Check for scholarships, employer tuition assistance, loan forgiveness, sponsored pathways, payment plans, tax benefits and aid that could cut the out-of-pocket cost before deciding on the sticker price.

codes.label: Cheaper or different credentials
codes.definition: Compare the program with lower-cost or more targeted options such as certificates, cheaper programs, employer-sponsored training or other credentials that might achieve the same goal.

codes.label: Whether the credential serves a specific career goal
codes.definition: Decide whether the degree is a means to a defined role or target path and whether that path actually requires or rewards it, rather than pursuing it as a generic credential.

codes.label: Realistic salary and job market
codes.definition: Verify that the projected post-degree salary and job openings are realistic locally, including specialty, setting, new-graduate versus experienced pay, and how long it takes to land the role.

codes.label: Employer's valuation and internal advancement
codes.definition: Consider whether the current employer would promote or pay more for the degree, or whether an internal advancement route exists that makes the degree less necessary.

codes.label: Program quality, accreditation and outcomes
codes.definition: Verify accreditation, reputation, alumni network, graduate pass rates and job placement results, since the credential's value depends on them.

codes.label: Clinical placement and scheduling logistics
codes.definition: Determine how required practical hours or placements will be arranged around work and family, whether the program supports finding sites, and whether the employer will flex schedules or grant leave.

codes.label: Time load and burnout risk
codes.definition: Estimate the total study and work hours over the program and honestly assess whether the combined load is sustainable without burnout or dropout.

codes.label: Health, sleep and fatigue
codes.definition: Consider the physical and mental strain, including sleep deprivation and patient or performance safety, of stacking study on top of demanding work.

codes.label: Impact on partner and relationship
codes.definition: Weigh the time away from a partner, especially in the early years of marriage, and how evenings and weekends consumed by study affect the relationship.

codes.label: Partner involvement in the decision
codes.definition: The decision commits shared finances and time, so the partner's income, goals, risk tolerance and explicit agreement should be part of it.

codes.label: Impact on children and parenting
codes.definition: Consider how reduced availability affects children's supervision, emotional needs, routines and transportation during the program, including the timing relative to their ages.

codes.label: Childcare and support network
codes.definition: Identify concrete backup help such as family, friends or paid childcare for gaps, illness or schedule collisions before committing.

codes.label: Deadline pressure and deferral options
codes.definition: Treat a short deposit deadline as pressure that may distort the decision, and check whether the deposit is refundable and whether deferral or a later start is possible.

codes.label: Reversibility and withdrawal costs
codes.definition: Consider what would be owed or lost if you withdrew partway, and whether the decision can be undone or tested more cheaply first.

codes.label: Timing relative to other life plans
codes.definition: Consider how the multi-year program overlaps with plans such as marriage, children, home buying or relocation, and whether waiting would be better.

codes.label: Role change, responsibility and job fit
codes.definition: Weigh whether the day-to-day work of the new role, including greater autonomy, liability, accountability and administrative load, actually suits her or him compared with the current role.

codes.label: Motivation, identity and long-term satisfaction
codes.definition: Reflect on whether the move is pulled by a real goal or pushed by exhaustion or anxiety, and how the credential changes self-concept, network and satisfaction beyond salary.

codes.label: Job security, seniority and benefits at risk
codes.definition: Consider hidden value in the current job, such as seniority, schedule control, pension accruals, health insurance and benefits, that could be lost or disrupted by changing roles or hours.

codes.label: Retirement timeline and career horizon
codes.definition: Weigh how many working years remain to benefit from the higher earnings, and how the move and its cost affect retirement savings and long-term security.

codes.label: Licensure and state requirements
codes.definition: Check state licensure, certification exams, scope-of-practice rules and portability, which determine whether the credential is usable and marketable.

codes.label: Sunk-cost trap
codes.definition: Avoid treating a paid deposit or committed spending as a reason to continue; judge the program by what it adds going forward.

codes.label: Opportunity cost of study time
codes.definition: Weigh what the years of evenings and weekends spent in class and studying could otherwise produce, such as side income, savings building, rest, other certifications or skill-building.

codes.label: Existing experience as an advantage
codes.definition: Recognize that years of relevant professional experience can ease admission, make the transition smoother, build credibility and speed productivity in the new role, which lowers the risk compared with starting from scratch.

codes.label: Reduced personal commitments and household responsibilities
codes.definition: Consider which hobbies, social activities and household tasks would have to be cut or redistributed during the program, and whether family members, such as older children, could realistically take on more at home.

codes.label: Cost of staying put
codes.definition: Treat declining or deferring as a choice with its own costs, such as health strain from the current schedule, limited schedule control and a capped earning ceiling, rather than assuming it is the risk-free default.
